P1.evidence: The title carries the KFS setter suffix, so the read-back check applies and it was not done — no application, no setter notes and no reference to any prior conversation, on a call where the prospect had come through a webinar. The frame was the usual three parts: 'It's an opportunity for me to understand you. Where are you today? Where do you want to be? If we can help, I can go over some options' — 'what's in the way' omitted, which is the element that matters most for a man whose entire story is about what gets in the way. Agreement was the trailing 'Okay'. The open question was clean: 'How can we potentially help you, Mario?'

P2.evidence: Uneven, with one genuinely strong check. P2d is the best injury discovery in the entire folder and should be clipped for training: 'You mentioned the shoulder a couple of times now' becomes 'how long did you say this cycle of injuries has been going on for?', then 'you're 58 today, is that like 10 years, 15?', then 'you used an interesting adjective. You said vicious. What's been the most vicious part for you about this cycle?' It produced the sciatic nerve, the tennis elbow, the right shoulder and hip, the twenty-year-old back injury, and the specific recent episode with pull-ups and halos. Against that, the rep declared the baseline complete before he had it — 'I think we've got a good baseline there for you, Mario' at 00:03:46 — and age, height and weight all arrived unprompted afterwards. Health conditions were never asked, so the heart-attack risk and raised blood pressure came out only inside a story. Occupation was asked at 00:26:46, more than halfway through the pillar block. Diet was engaged with rather than elicited — the 22-hour fast, the carnivore pattern and the two pounds of meat a day were all volunteered, though the rep did probe with 'Every day?' and 'How do you feel?'. Sleep and energy were never raised at all, in a 58-year-old with chronic pain who fasts 22 hours a day.

P3.evidence: Strong throughout and outstanding in one stretch. The golden-years question opened it — 'You said something very striking a second ago. You said you want to enjoy your golden years. What does that look like for you?' — and produced the Camino de Santiago, Mount Whitney, working with his hands, and getting his wife hiking. The bridge past the physical landed the best answer on the call: 'what is still driving you to get out of this cycle and to enjoy your golden years?' — 'I want to see how close I can get to 100 years of age.' The who-else move was asked twice and is where the call becomes exceptional: 'have others noticed this cycle for yourself?' produced 'No... I don't even mention it to anybody', and the follow-up — 'carrying that inside, no one else knowing, what has that been like for yourself for the best part of over a decade, decade and a half?' — is the single best question anyone asks in this folder. The identity drive reached faith, his three children and 'just want to make sure that the second half of my life is better than the first half'. The reflect-back was lighter than it should have been, delivered as a repeated refrain about golden years rather than a confirmed restatement.

P4.evidence: Past attempts and root cause both ran well. CrossFit, the Trevor movements, the push-up and pull-up and halo protocol were all surfaced along with what happened to each — CrossFit 'was tearing up my body', the sciatic injury from adding weight, the shoulder from adding pull-ups. The blocker question was asked cleanly: 'Aside from the cycle of injuries, is there anything else that could really stop you from stepping into your healthier version of you?' The prospect named the real gap himself, which is self-regulation rather than knowledge: 'Maybe I wanted the results faster than what it should be. I went up in weight, and I was doing it, and then I hurt my sciatic nerve.' The only miss is the information-isn't-the-problem challenge, which was never run here — reasonably, since this prospect's problem is demonstrably not a lack of information.

P5.evidence: The settle-for move is the sharpest instance of it in this batch and it worked. Off the back of a want-not-need answer: 'The fact that you said it's a want and not a need makes me realize that you are kind of okay settling with the aches and pains. You've become comfortable with it' — which drew the admission 'yeah, I've had my shoulder pain forever... they're almost like, I don't want to say my BFFs'. He then asked permission to be blunt and delivered it: 'if this isn't a need, nothing is going to change.' The line in the sand followed properly — 'So you're actually ready to take that step, Mario?' — 'Let's do it.' What is missing is the horizon. There is no 'if nothing changes, what does life look like in two years', which on a man three to four years from retirement with a bucket-list 500-mile walk was the most powerful question available on this call and was never asked. The why-not was pursued only through the generic comfort-zone framing.

P6.evidence: Correctly sequenced and correctly handled. The trust gauge ran before any price and returned 'needing you guys is a 10', with the hesitation surfaced honestly in the same breath — 'will I be able to do it with my little injuries here and there?' The rep addressed it rather than skating past it, then ran the capability check explicitly: 'Do you feel internally capable of getting out of this cycle of injuries and actually enjoying your golden years if you do the right thing? That's really important for me to know.' — 'Yes.' A clear yes existed before the offer. The all-in question was never asked, which is why the household spending rule and the house purchase both arrived after the price rather than before it; that is the one omission that cost him a same-call decision.

P11.evidence: No agreement was reached on the call — the prospect asked for an hour to speak with his wife — so payment, the Trevor booking, the agreement email and the onboarding sequence were all unreachable. The rep confirmed his personal mobile number for the follow-up text.

objection_plays.detail: A textbook trigger with a hard number attached: 'my wife and I have this thing where we talk about it before... anything over a thousand dollars, we need to talk about it before.' Ran: the permission-versus-input distinction almost verbatim — 'is it just a situation where you're letting her know, hey honey, this is what I'm going to do for my health, or is it asking, hey honey, do you think I should do this?' — the obstacles question in substance, via the sticker-shock discussion, and the devil's-advocate refusal scenario: 'despite all of that, she says no. What do you feel like you're going to do?' Not run, and this is the important part: 'Money aside, do you personally feel this CAN get you to your goal?' and above all 'Is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain?' — a move written for precisely this man, who has hidden fifteen years of pain from her and whose wife has just been given hiking boots so she can join him. The scripted fallback of a refundable deposit was also not used; the rep substituted the $1,200 trial, which does not clear the $1,000 household threshold that created the objection in the first place.

Money was flagged early and unprompted — 'The other part could be financial, you know' at 00:15:28 — and then confirmed with specifics: a house purchase in progress, a history of serious debt now cleared, and a stated spending threshold. Not one move of the play ran. No isolation, no HOW-not-SHOULD frame, no permission question, and none of the six financial-picture questions, despite in-house payment plans being mentioned in the same breath as the price. Had the isolation question been asked at 00:15:28, the spousal rule would have surfaced twenty minutes before the offer instead of immediately after it.

Fear was named by both parties and is the true blocker on this call: 'my hesitation is, will I be able to do it with my little injuries?' and earlier, when asked what holds people back, 'Fear... Because I've lived it.' Ran: the fear-of-failure-or-success framing, the comfort-zone sequence, and the audit-and-no-rush reassurance. Not run: the certainty question, the BRIDGE, the PLANE, and most conspicuously BURNED BEFORE — 'if you got hurt in a relationship once, do you never trust again?' — which is the exact play for a man who has been physically hurt by training every four to five months for fifteen years. It was available and unused.

SCRIPT GAP — clinical fit, fourth instance in this batch and the most acute. The prospect stated a hard, current physical exclusion: 'if you tell me, do a burpee, I can't. That'll trigger my sciatic nerve', on top of an active tennis elbow, a right shoulder that has stopped his push-ups, and sciatica resolved three weeks earlier. The playbook offers nothing, so the rep improvised the baseline audit as the answer. The move that does not exist and was needed here is: pause, get these four injuries assessed by a clinician, and close conditionally on that. Note this is the strongest case in the corpus for building it, because the prospect's most recent injury was caused by attempting this company's own published movements.

SCRIPT GAP — the competitor that delivered the model and injured him. CrossFit gave him a meal plan, class structure and real accountability including chase-up calls, and he lost weight on it. Two things were true at once and neither was addressed: it proved the model works on him, and it hurt him. 'They developed a meal plan for me, I followed the meal plan, I went in, did their exercises, and then the accountability was there, because if I don't go to class, they're going to call me' sits alongside 'it was tearing up my body. I just could not keep up.' There is no play for differentiating against a competitor whose only failure was load management, which is precisely what this programme claims to solve.

notes: The first twenty minutes are the best discovery in this folder and the injury sequence and the 'what has that been like, carrying it alone' question should both be used as training material. Two corrections. First and most serious: the rep elicited a complete, alarming injury history — four active sites, a fifteen-year pattern, and a man who cannot do a burpee — and then used none of it as a gate, moving instead to a therapeutic assurance that 'any pains that you're experiencing are naturally going to be subsided.' The correct output of that discovery was a clearance condition, and the playbook gives him no way to write one. Second: the money isolation was skipped at 00:15:28 when the prospect flagged finances himself, so the household spending rule arrived after the price rather than before it, and the response was a $1,200 trial that still exceeds the $1,000 threshold it was meant to solve.
